title: Chapter II

teacherSummary.text: Victor recalls his friend Henry Clerval and his own early fascination with the alchemists Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus and Albertus Magnus. A lightning strike that destroys an oak tree introduces him to electricity, and he briefly turns to mathematics before 'destiny' pulls him back.

vocabulary.context: Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.

context.history: Agrippa and Paracelsus were Renaissance figures who mixed early science with magic. Lightning and electricity fascinated Enlightenment scientists like Benjamin Franklin.

significance: Victor frames his life as fated, shifting responsibility away from his choices—a key point for discussion.
discussionQuestions: Victor blames 'destiny' for his fate. Do you agree, or did he choose?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with isolation and the need for companionship?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter II,” how does Shelley show the first spark of obsession? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter II develops the idea of the first spark of obsession. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses foreshadowing in Chapter II to complicate the reader's understanding of the first spark of obsession. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter II within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the first spark of obsession responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter II as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the first spark of obsession. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage: The untaught peasant beheld the elements around him, and was acquainted with their practical uses. The most learned philosopher knew little more. He had partially unveiled the face of Nature, but her immortal lineaments were still a wonder and a mystery. He might dissect, anatomise, and give names; but, not to speak of a final cause, causes in their secondary and tertiary grades were utterly unknown to him. I had gazed upon the fortifications and impediments that seemed to keep human beings from entering the citadel of nature, and rashly and ignorantly I had repined.

segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Victor blames 'destiny' for his fate. Do you agree, or did he choose? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include ligaments, disunion, loudness, preceptors, dissect. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Thus strangely are our souls constructed, and by such slight ligaments are we bound to prosperity or ruin.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: Anything that ties or unites one thing or part to another.

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Agrippa and Paracelsus were Renaissance figures who mixed early science with magic. Lightning and electricity fascinated Enlightenment scientists like Benjamin Franklin. Now, why does this chapter matter? Victor frames his life as fated, shifting responsibility away from his choices—a key point for discussion. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Symbolism.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot foreshadowing, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
